extracted_claims.text: Article 43 provides two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control (Annex VI, self-assessment) or quality management system plus technical documentation assessment by a notified body (Annex VII).

Annex VII (third-party notified body assessment) is mandatory for biometric identification systems listed in point 1 of Annex III and for certain high-risk AI systems embedded as safety components in products covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation (points 2-8), unless harmonised standards/common specifications have been applied, in which case internal control may be used.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, providers must follow the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies ensuring AI-specific requirements are also checked.
Substantial modifications to a high-risk AI system require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority to authorise placing on the market or putting into service of a specific high-risk AI system for a limited period, as a derogation from the Article 43 conformity assessment, for exceptional reasons of public security, life/health protection, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Providers may choose any notified body for the Annex VII conformity assessment, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or by Union institutions/bodies/offices/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority under Article 74(8) or (9) acts as the notified body instead.

Annex VII section 4.5 permits a notified body, where necessary and after other means have been exhausted, to request access to the training and trained models of the AI system (subject to IP and confidentiality protections) to assess conformity.
Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes the administrative framework for assigning identification numbers and publishing lists of notified bodies.

A Council document (dated 2026) references Article 30 of a regulation setting the scope of designation of conformity assessment bodies notified for AI systems, with AIP codes mapping to categories under Annex I of the AI Act.

A Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would amend the framework to add a new Annex XIV listing codes/types of AI systems for the NANDO notified/designated organisations system, and would also amend Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements.

As of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated under the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) in the NANDO database; the CRA sets a target of 11 December 2026 for sufficient notified body capacity, with full application from 11 December 2027.

As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem specifically for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act for medical device AI systems (MDR/IVDR interplay).

High-risk AI obligations under the AI Act are stated to fully apply from August 2026, after which notified bodies designated under the AI Act would begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments (distinct from existing MDR/IVDR notified body assessments).
As of October 2025, the NANDO system listed 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies (these are medical-device-specific designations, not AI Act designations).

The Commission's European Approach to AI document (Oct 2021) and a November 2022 proposal text of Article 43 reflect an early/proposal-stage version of the conformity assessment provisions, prior to the final adopted AI Act text.

Most high-risk AI systems not embedded in regulated products under Annex I can use the internal control (self-assessment) procedure under Annex VI; third-party notified body assessment under Annex VII is required primarily for biometric identification and certain safety-component systems.

The Commission may adopt delegated acts under Article 43(5) (via Article 97) to update Annex VI and Annex VII procedures in light of technical progress, and certification decisions are issued by notified bodies.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems—internal control self-assessment (Annex VI) and third-party notified body assessment (Annex VII)—with the latter mandatory primarily for biometric identification systems and certain regulated product safety components ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). However, the actual designation of notified bodies specifically under the AI Act remains largely unconfirmed in available sources: two single-source, undated, low-confidence (0.12) blog posts suggest that as of early-to-mid 2026 the AI Act notified-body ecosystem was still underdeveloped, but this should not be read as a corroborated consensus, since the underlying evidence is thin and inconsistent (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act provides two pathways for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI (provider self-assessment), or a combination of quality management system review and technical documentation assessment by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). Annex VII third-party assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems listed in Annex III point 1 and for high-risk systems embedded as safety components in products under Annex I harmonisation legislation (points 2–8), unless harmonised standards have been applied, permitting internal control instead (high confidence) ([futurium.ec.europa.eu](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). For most other high-risk systems not embedded in regulated products, internal control (self-assessment) is expected to be the dominant route (low confidence) ([Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

Where AI systems are covered by existing EU sectoral product legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorise temporary derogations from conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII, notified bodies may, as a last resort and subject to IP/confidentiality safeguards, request access to training data and trained models (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). The Commission also retains power under Article 43(5), exercised via Article 97, to adopt delegated acts updating the Annex VI and Annex VII procedures in light of technical progress, with certification decisions remaining the responsibility of notified bodies (low confidence) ([FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

### Notified Body Selection and Designation Framework
Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions—in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Article 35 establishes the administrative framework for assigning identification numbers and publishing notified body lists (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)). A 2026 Council document references an Article 30 framework and "AIP codes" mapping designation scope to Annex I categories (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)), while a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would add a new Annex XIV for NANDO system codes and integrate AI Act requirements into aviation safety regulation (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Current Designation Status (Low Confidence, Timeline Uncertain)
Two low-confidence, single-source blogs suggest the AI Act notified body ecosystem remained underdeveloped as of early-to-mid 2026: one states that as of March 2026 designation processes were still ongoing across Member States with limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), and another states no notified bodies had been designated for medical device AI systems as of April 2026 ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). A separate source indicates AI Act-specific designation activity is expected only after high-risk obligations take effect in August 2026 ([mdxcro.com](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd)). By comparison, NANDO listed 51 MDR and 19 IVDR notified bodies as of October 2025—but these are medical-device-specific, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). As further context on the broader EU notified-body ecosystem, a separate low-confidence report states that zero notified bodies had been designated under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) as of late June 2026, with the CRA targeting sufficient notified-body capacity by December 2026 and full application from December 2027 ([cybercertlabs.com](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026))—illustrating that slow notified-body ramp-up is a pattern across recent EU digital/product regulations, not unique to the AI Act.

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the precise timing of AI Act notified body designation relative to the August 2026 deadline; the eyreACT and aiact-navigator claims (confidence 0.12 each) rely on single, undated, non-authoritative blog sources and should not be treated as corroborated findings. The Council/Commission framework documents on Article 30/AIP codes and Annex XIV (confidence 0.68) are more authoritative but do not confirm actual designation outcomes. Earlier Commission proposal texts (2021–2022) for Article 43 may not reflect the final adopted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, risking conflation of draft and final law.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms a current, definitive list of notified bodies designated specifically under the AI Act. It remains unclear how the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO amendments interact with actual designation timelines, what happens if no notified bodies are available by August 2026 for Annex VII-required systems, and how the Council's Article 30/AIP code framework reconciles with Article 43/35 provisions. The CRA designation delays raise an open question about whether similar bottlenecks will affect AI Act notified-body availability, but no source directly addresses this linkage.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems—internal control self-assessment (Annex VI) and third-party notified body assessment (Annex VII)—with the latter mandatory primarily for biometric identification systems and certain regulated product safety components ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). However, the actual designation of notified bodies specifically under the AI Act remains largely unconfirmed in available sources, with multiple reports indicating that as of early-to-mid 2026 no AI Act-specific notified bodies had yet been formally designated, even as the August 2026 high-risk obligations deadline approached (medium/low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act provides two pathways for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI (provider self-assessment), or a combination of quality management system review and technical documentation assessment by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). Annex VII third-party assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems listed in Annex III point 1 and for high-risk systems embedded as safety components in products under Annex I harmonisation legislation (points 2–8), unless harmonised standards have been applied, permitting internal control instead (high confidence) ([futurium.ec.europa.eu](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). For most other high-risk systems not embedded in regulated products, internal control (self-assessment) is expected to be the dominant route (low confidence) ([Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

Where AI systems are covered by existing EU sectoral product legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorise temporary derogations from conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII, notified bodies may, as a last resort and subject to IP/confidentiality safeguards, request access to training data and trained models (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Selection and Designation Framework
Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions—in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Article 35 establishes the administrative framework for assigning identification numbers and publishing notified body lists (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)). A 2026 Council document references an Article 30 framework and "AIP codes" mapping designation scope to Annex I categories (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)), while a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would add a new Annex XIV for NANDO system codes and integrate AI Act requirements into aviation safety regulation (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Current Designation Status (Low Confidence, Timeline Uncertain)
Multiple low-confidence sources suggest that, as of early-to-mid 2026, the AI Act notified body ecosystem remained underdeveloped: one source states no notified bodies had been designated for medical device AI systems as of April 2026 ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)), while another indicates designation activity begins only after high-risk obligations take effect in August 2026 ([mdxcro.com](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd)). By comparison, NANDO listed 51 MDR and 19 IVDR notified bodies as of October 2025—but these are medical-device-specific, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the precise timing of AI Act notified body designation relative to the August 2026 deadline, with low-confidence claims offering inconsistent pictures. Several low-confidence claims (0.12–0.20) regarding designation timelines and the Council/Commission framework documents should be treated cautiously, as they rely on single, undated, non-authoritative sources. Earlier Commission proposal texts (2021–2022) for Article 43 may not reflect the final adopted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, risking conflation of draft and final law.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms a current, definitive list of notified bodies designated specifically under the AI Act. It remains unclear how the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO amendments interact with actual designation timelines, what happens if no notified bodies are available by August 2026 for Annex VII-required systems, and how the Council's Article 30/AIP code framework reconciles with Article 43/35 provisions.

Two low-confidence, single-source blogs suggest the AI Act notified body ecosystem remained underdeveloped as of early-to-mid 2026: one states that as of March 2026 designation processes were still ongoing across Member States with limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), and another states no notified bodies had been designated for medical device AI systems as of April 2026 ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). No source confirms a current, definitive list of notified bodies designated specifically under the AI Act.
